hero.headline: Judge orders national parks to restore exhibits on slavery and climate change
hero.body:
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to restore signs and exhibits at national parks that address topics including slavery and climate change. The ruling blocks the removal of educational materials that had been targeted under a recent executive directive.

The order requires officials to re-install displays that had been taken down from parks across the country. The affected exhibits include historical information about slavery and environmental content related to climate change. Multiple national park sites had begun removing or covering such materials following the administration's directive.

The judge's decision halts what the court characterized as censorship of park exhibits. The ruling comes after challenges were filed against the removal policy, with plaintiffs arguing that the directive violated educational and historical preservation mandates. The order applies to materials that had been removed or were scheduled for removal under the executive action.

National parks serve as educational institutions that preserve and interpret American history and natural resources for millions of visitors annually. The affected exhibits provide context about historical events and scientific information that parks have traditionally presented as part of their mission. The removal of such materials had drawn objections from historians, scientists, and park advocacy groups.

The Trump administration has not yet indicated whether it will appeal the ruling. Park officials must now work to restore the removed materials to their original locations. The decision represents a significant check on the executive directive and affirms the role of national parks in presenting comprehensive historical and scientific information to the public.

cards.headline: Iran and US near agreement to end fighting and reopen Strait of Hormuz
cards.body:
The United States and Iran say they are close to finalizing a deal to end hostilities, with both sides indicating that an agreement would lead to the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Pakistan has been mediating the negotiations between Washington and Tehran. However, the situation remains volatile, with recent military actions raising questions about whether peace talks will ultimately succeed.

The strait is a critical global shipping route through which roughly one-fifth of the world's oil supply passes. Disruptions to this waterway have caused significant economic strain worldwide, with countries dependent on Gulf oil facing fuel shortages and price increases.

Recent developments have complicated negotiations. Iran's parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said that reopening the strait would be "impossible" while the US and Israel committed what he called "flagrant" breaches of any ceasefire agreement. He specifically cited a US naval blockade that he described as "the hostage-taking of the world's economy."

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps seized two ships in the strait, claiming they were attempting to cross covertly. The Panama-flagged MSC Francesca and Liberia-flagged Epaminondas were brought to shore. Greece's foreign minister confirmed that an attack occurred against the Greek-operated Epaminondas. A maritime security monitor also reported that another vessel was fired upon by an Iranian gunboat, sustaining heavy damage.

The US has imposed its own blockade on Iran, which the White House said has cost Iran approximately $500 million daily. Trump announced he was extending a ceasefire unilaterally while simultaneously threatening military action, creating uncertainty about American intentions.

The economic consequences of the strait's closure have been severe. Germany halved its 2026 growth forecast to 0.5 percent, while Greece announced 500 million euros in additional aid for households and farmers. The International Maritime Organization reported that approximately 20,000 seafarers and 2,000 ships have been stranded in the Gulf.

Planned peace talks in Islamabad were abandoned when Iran did not publicly accept the invitation and the US delegation led by Vice President JD Vance never departed Washington. A Pakistani official told Reuters that preparations had been completed but the cancelled talks represented an unexpected setback.

Prior attempts at diplomatic resolution have failed. Trump withdrew from Iran's nuclear agreement during his first term, a decision he was encouraged to make by Israel. Years of tension have now escalated into open conflict.

A secondary conflict between Israel and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah has also complicated regional stability. A ceasefire between these parties is set to expire, with Israeli strikes continuing despite the temporary agreement. A journalist and photographer were killed in Lebanon on Wednesday during an Israeli airstrike.

cards.headline: Trump tells Netanyahu he expects to sign Iran deal within days
cards.teaser: President informs Israeli prime minister of impending agreement, signaling end to joint military campaign.
cards.body:
President Trump called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday evening to inform him he expected to sign a deal with Iran within days. Trump told Netanyahu the agreement was final and it was time to end the war, according to a senior U.S. official. The call delivered news Netanyahu did not want to hear about the direction of U.S. policy.

Netanyahu had hoped the war would lead to regime change in Tehran when he joined military operations alongside Trump. The prime minister faces an election four months away and had envisioned a different outcome from the campaign. The pending agreement represents a shift in U.S. approach toward Iran and ends the joint military effort that Netanyahu had supported.

cards.headline: Trump announces US military killed Venezuelan gang leader in strike
cards.teaser: President Trump announced late Friday that U.S.
cards.body:
President Trump announced Friday that U.S. Southern Command conducted a strike that killed Niño Guerrero, leader of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua. Trump described it as a "swift and lethal kinetic strike" and shared a video appearing to show the airstrike on his Truth Social platform.

Tren de Aragua originated in Venezuela and has expanded operations across multiple countries. The gang has been linked to human trafficking, drug smuggling, and violent crime across South America and the United States, prompting increased concern from U.S. law enforcement and national security officials.

cards.headline: Justice Department approves $111 billion Paramount-Warner Bros. merger
cards.teaser: Federal regulators cleared the combination of two major Hollywood studios after an eight-month antitrust review.
cards.body:
The Trump administration's Department of Justice has approved the $111 billion merger between Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery, clearing a major regulatory obstacle for the deal. The antitrust division completed its review after an eight-month investigation, determining that the transaction poses no competitive threat.

The Justice Department stated that it "received from the Parties over two million documents from over 80 custodians, substantial productions of data, as well as extensive documents, data, and advocacy from third parties across the media and entertainment ecosystem." Based on this review, regulators concluded the merger is unlikely to harm competition or consumers in streaming video on demand, linear television, or theatrical film distribution.

The combination will unite two major film studios and place CNN under the same corporate umbrella as CBS News. Paramount stated that the deal is "pro-competitive, resulting in a stronger company better positioned to compete against dominant technology platforms in an industry increasingly defined by intense competition for audiences, talent, technology, and investment."

However, significant obstacles remain. The UK Competition and Markets Authority opened an investigation into the merger and set an August 7 deadline to determine whether a more in-depth review is necessary. European regulators are also investigating the funding behind the merger, which includes $24 billion in commitments from three Gulf sovereign-wealth funds. Australia already approved the deal, and numerous other countries have provided clearance.

Concerns persist among journalists and industry observers. Staff members at both CBS News and CNN have expressed worry about potential job losses, as the companies have promised $6 billion in synergies from the deal. Some CNN staffers have also voiced concerns about editorial direction, given that the Ellison family, which controls Paramount, has close ties to the Trump administration. While David Ellison pledged in March that CNN's editorial independence would be protected, speculation continues about potential leadership changes.

A coalition of U.S. state attorneys general could still file a lawsuit to block the merger. California Attorney General Rob Bonta indicated Friday that the deal "remains under investigation by my office" and stressed that it is "not a done deal."

Opponents criticized the approval decision. Craig Aaron, co-chief executive of Free Press, said that "the fix was in at the Trump Justice Department from the start." Senator Elizabeth Warren called the approval "terrible news for every American who doesn't want Trump-aligned billionaires to control what they watch and how much they pay," adding that the merger "has reeked of corruption and influence-peddling."

The Justice Department's decision represents a significant step toward completing the transaction, but legal challenges and international scrutiny could still affect the merger's final outcome.

cards.headline: Trump administration blocks foreign access to Anthropic's most powerful AI models
cards.teaser: The AI company disabled global access to its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 systems following a government directive.
cards.body:
Anthropic halted foreign access to its most advanced artificial intelligence models after receiving orders from the Trump administration. The company disabled its Fable 5 and Mythos 5 systems for users outside the United States to comply with the government directive.

The move represents a significant shift in AI policy, restricting access to cutting-edge technology on national security grounds. Anthropic confirmed it took the action in response to the government order, though the company has not detailed the specific rationale provided by officials.

cards.headline: FISA surveillance authority expires as Section 702 reaches end of authorization
cards.teaser: Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act expired Friday night, though existing surveillance certifications remain valid until March 2027.
cards.body:
Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act reached its expiration date on Friday night. The provision has allowed intelligence agencies to conduct surveillance operations without individual warrants under certain conditions.

Despite the expiration of the legal authority, surveillance activities will continue under existing certifications that remain valid until March 2027. The gap between the law's expiration and the end of operational authority means intelligence collection will proceed for months. Section 702 has generated ongoing debate over privacy protections and government surveillance powers.

cards.headline: UAE to release billions to Iran in effort to halt attacks, reports say
cards.teaser: The United Arab Emirates will unlock billions of dollars for Iran as part of a major shift aimed at stopping attacks, according to multiple reports.
cards.body:
The UAE government has denied reports of a $3 billion transfer to Iran, according to Anadolu Agency. However, multiple outlets including The Times of Israel and Yahoo reported that the UAE plans to release substantial funds to Iran as part of efforts to de-escalate regional tensions.

UAE and Iranian officials have held face-to-face meetings to discuss reducing conflict, Bloomberg reported. According to BBC News, the US, Iran, and mediators Pakistan say a deal to end hostilities is close to being finalized, with potential benefits including the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

cards.headline: Switzerland to vote on proposal to cap population at 10 million
cards.teaser: Swiss voters will decide on what would be the world's first national population cap, with Switzerland proposing to limit its population to 10 million people.
cards.body:
The BBC and Wall Street Journal reported that Switzerland will hold a referendum on capping the country's population at 10 million. The right-wing Swiss People's Party is promoting the measure as a "sustainability initiative," though opponents argue it would create chaos.

The proposal has ignited debate over immigration policy and economic growth. Basel, Switzerland's pharmaceutical hub, has expressed concerns about how a population cap could affect the region's development and business environment.

cards.headline: European Union launches membership talks with Ukraine and Moldova
cards.teaser: EU envoys agreed to begin the first phase of accession negotiations with Ukraine and Moldova, advancing both countries' bids to join the bloc.
cards.body:
The European Union has agreed to begin accession talks with Ukraine and Moldova, marking the start of their formal membership process. EU envoys greenlit the first phase of these negotiations for both countries.

Ukrainian President Zelenskyy characterized the opening of EU accession talks as significant support for Ukraine, particularly as the country continues its war with Russia.

cards.headline: US deports Iranian activist to Central African Republic
cards.teaser: The United States deported an Iranian pro-democracy activist to the Central African Republic, according to the activist's lawyer.
cards.body:
Reuters and Fox News reported that the Trump administration deported the Iranian activist to the violence-plagued Central African nation under a new agreement. The New York Times said women who fled Iran were among those to be deported to the Central African Republic.

CBS News reported that the US is deporting migrants from Afghanistan, Iran, and other countries to the Central African Republic, a nation experiencing ongoing conflict. The deportations raised questions about sending individuals to a country with severe security problems.

cards.headline: Afghans stage rare public protests against Taliban restrictions
cards.teaser: Dozens of women were arrested and two people were killed during uncommon public demonstrations against Taliban rules in Afghanistan.
cards.body:
The United Nations said it was deeply concerned about the arrests of dozens of women during the protests. The demonstrations, organized to support women's rights, represent a rare instance of public opposition to Taliban governance.

Two people were killed during the protests, according to UN reports. The protests highlight ongoing tensions in Afghanistan over restrictions imposed by the Taliban government since it took power.

cards.headline: Pope Leo borrows Spanish king's aircraft after mechanical failure
cards.teaser: Pope Leo had to use an aircraft provided by Spain's king to return to the Vatican after his plane experienced engine problems.
cards.body:
The Washington Post and AP News reported that Pope Leo's flight home from Spain was grounded due to a mechanical issue. The king of Spain offered his aircraft to help the pontiff complete his journey. Vatican News confirmed that Pope Leo returned to the Vatican on the Spanish monarch's plane.

According to Reuters, the papal aircraft remained in Spain while maintenance crews addressed the technical problems. The pope used the borrowed jet to resume his travels to Rome following the mechanical failure.

cards.headline: US military kills Tren de Aragua gang leader in airstrike
cards.teaser: President Trump announced the US military conducted a strike that killed the leader of the Venezuelan gang.
cards.body:
President Trump announced that the US military killed Niño Guerrero, leader of Venezuela's Tren de Aragua criminal organization, in what he described as a "swift and lethal kinetic strike." Trump posted a video on Truth Social appearing to show the airstrike.

The Venezuelan gang has operated across multiple countries in the Americas. Trump indicated that Venezuela cooperated with the military operation targeting the gang's leadership.

cards.headline: Major warehouse fire in Tracy burns as one of largest in US
cards.teaser: A fire at a California warehouse complex has prompted evacuations and could continue burning for days.
cards.body:
A massive fire at a warehouse complex in Tracy, California has been described by officials as one of the largest in the United States. The blaze has prompted evacuations of nearby areas as firefighters work to contain it. Officials warn the fire could continue burning for several days.

The sprinkler system at the Medline facility failed to activate during the fire. Authorities have warned residents not to touch debris from the fire, stating that material could be hazardous. Health officials have urged precautions as smoke from the fire spreads through the air.

cards.headline: Judge blocks Trump administration payout fund indefinitely
cards.teaser: A federal judge has extended an order blocking an $1.8 billion fund intended for those claiming government weaponization.
cards.body:
A federal judge in Virginia has extended an order blocking the Trump administration's $1.8 billion fund designed to compensate alleged victims of government weaponization. Judge Leonie Brinkema said the administration's public statements that the fund was dead were insufficient to convince her it would not proceed.

The judge offered a path to lift the block: if the acting attorney general Todd Blanche and treasury secretary Scott Bessent file sworn declarations under penalty of perjury within a week stating the fund will not move forward, she would dismiss the case. The fund was created partly to resolve Trump's lawsuit against the IRS over leaked tax returns.

cards.headline: Kennedy Center removes Trump's name from building
cards.teaser: A court-ordered deadline required the removal of references to President Trump from the Kennedy Center.
cards.body:
Scaffolding was erected at the Kennedy Center as workers prepared to remove President Trump's name from the building. A federal judge rejected an emergency request to delay the court-ordered deadline set for Friday. The Kennedy Center's subsequent appeal was also denied Friday evening.

Despite the last-minute legal challenges, the removal proceeded as scheduled. Workers returned to the building Friday evening as crowds gathered to watch the planned removal of Trump's name from the institution.

cards.headline: Gene Shalit, longtime Today show movie critic, dies at 100
cards.teaser: The film critic known for his distinctive appearance and wordplay spent decades as Today's arts editor.
cards.body:
Gene Shalit, the longtime movie critic and arts editor for the Today show, has died at age 100. He joined the program in 1970 and became arts editor in 1973, roles he maintained for over four decades. His family announced his death to NBC News, noting he "passed away peacefully today after 100 years of an amazing life."

Shalit became a beloved fixture on morning television, instantly recognizable for his distinctive puffy hair and oversized handlebar mustache. He earned a reputation as a witty and intelligent middle-of-the-road critic, often entertaining audiences with his affection for puns—some more groan-inducing than others.

cards.headline: Palestine Action activists imprisoned after factory raid classified as terrorism
cards.teaser: Convictions for criminal damage were classified as terrorism in what is believed to be a first for such cases.
cards.body:
Palestine Action activists have been jailed following a factory raid. The case represents a significant legal development, marking what is believed to be the first time that convictions for criminal damage have been classified as terrorism offenses.

The terrorism designation represents a shift in how property damage related to activism is prosecuted, affecting both the convictions and sentencing handed down in this case.

cards.headline: SpaceX shares jump 19% in largest IPO ever, making Musk first trillionaire
cards.teaser: SpaceX began trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange Friday with shares rising 19 percent by the close, completing the largest initial public offering in history.
cards.body:
SpaceX made its stock market debut Friday on the Nasdaq, with shares closing up 19 percent. The company listed with a market value of $2.2 trillion, marking the largest initial public offering in history. Shares closed at $161 after opening at $135.

Elon Musk became the world's first trillionaire following the IPO, with a net worth of $1.11 trillion according to the Bloomberg rich list.

cards.headline: Dow closes higher on optimism over Iran negotiations
cards.teaser: Stock indexes rose as investors reacted to hopes of diplomatic progress with Iran.
cards.body:
Major stock indexes ended Friday's session with gains, driven by investor optimism about potential progress in negotiations with Iran. The Dow Jones Industrial Average posted increases as market participants responded to geopolitical developments. President Trump announced he had canceled planned strikes on Iran, stating that a peace deal was near.

SpaceX's market debut added to positive sentiment during the trading session, with the company's stock surging 19%. The combination of diplomatic prospects and strong technology sector performance supported the broader market rally.

cards.headline: John D. Rockefeller became America's first billionaire in 1916
cards.teaser: The Gilded Age oil baron reached the milestone more than a century before Musk's trillionaire status.
cards.body:
John D. Rockefeller, the oil baron who built Standard Oil during the Gilded Age, became America's first billionaire in 1916. His achievement marked a historic milestone in American wealth accumulation and drew significant media attention.

More than a century later, Elon Musk reached an even greater milestone, becoming the world's first trillionaire. His wealth surged following SpaceX's market debut on the Nasdaq, where the company was valued at $2.2 trillion. Like Rockefeller's achievement over 110 years ago, Musk's ascension generated widespread headlines.

cards.headline: SpaceX listing valued at $2.2 trillion in market debut
cards.teaser: The rocket company's stock market entrance set records for initial public offering size.
cards.body:
SpaceX made history with its listing on the Nasdaq, achieving a $2.2 trillion valuation in what ranks as the largest IPO ever. The blockbuster debut sent the stock soaring, with shares jumping nearly 30% on the day of listing.

The IPO has also made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire, with his wealth now valued at $1.11 trillion according to the Bloomberg rich list. The successful market debut is expected to pave the way for other major offerings from tech companies including OpenAI and Anthropic.

cards.headline: OpenAI and Anthropic may follow SpaceX with planned stock offerings
cards.teaser: The successful rocket company debut could accelerate IPO plans for major AI firms.
cards.body:
SpaceX's record-breaking market debut has sparked momentum for a wave of major technology IPOs. The rocket company listed on the Nasdaq with a $2.2 trillion valuation, with shares rising significantly on the first day of trading. This blockbuster performance is paving the way for upcoming public offerings from AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic.

The successful SpaceX listing reflects a shift in the IPO landscape, with a new generation of tech firms—dubbed MANGOS by some analysts—leading market debuts. Both OpenAI and Anthropic are among the companies expected to pursue stock market listings as they seek capital for continued development and growth.

hero.headline: Critical vulnerability in Oracle PeopleSoft software compromises hundreds of organizations
hero.teaser: A zero-day vulnerability in PeopleSoft has enabled attackers to steal gigabytes of data from organizations using the Oracle-owned software.
hero.body:
A previously unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software has affected hundreds of organizations, allowing attackers to extract large amounts of data. The security flaw has been classified as critical, representing one of the most serious types of vulnerabilities.

The zero-day designation means the vulnerability was exploited before Oracle or security researchers knew it existed. Organizations using PeopleSoft for human resources, financial management, and other enterprise functions have been exposed to data theft. The vulnerability enabled attackers to steal gigabytes of information from compromised systems.

cards.headline: SpaceX completes IPO, shares close up 19% in first day of trading
cards.teaser: SpaceX made its public market debut on Friday, with shares closing 19% above the initial offering price of $135.
cards.body:
SpaceX made its public market debut on Friday, with shares closing 19% above the $135 initial offering price. The successful IPO valued the company at $2.1 trillion, making Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire. The strong first-day performance reflects investor confidence in SpaceX's business model across rocket launches, satellite deployments, and its Starlink internet constellation.

The Nasdaq fast-tracked SpaceX's inclusion on the index, which guarantees significant buying pressure from tracker funds and other forced buyers. As a publicly traded company, SpaceX now faces quarterly earnings expectations and shareholder demands alongside its ambitious space exploration goals.

cards.headline: Google sues Chinese cybercrime group over AI-powered text message scams
cards.teaser: The tech company filed a lawsuit against an operation called Outsider Enterprise that used artificial intelligence to defraud hundreds of thousands of victims.
cards.body:
Google has filed a lawsuit against Outsider Enterprise, a Chinese cybercrime group that used artificial intelligence to conduct large-scale scam campaigns. The operation sent 2.5 million fraudulent text messages over just two weeks, targeting hundreds of thousands of victims.

The case highlights how AI technology can be weaponized to amplify the reach and speed of criminal schemes. By automating its messaging operations, the cybercrime group was able to scale its fraud efforts significantly, demonstrating the challenges that emerging technologies present for both consumers and tech companies.

cards.headline: Jeff Bezos launches Prometheus startup focused on physical AI applications
cards.teaser: The Amazon founder's new venture joins the field of companies developing AI systems that interact with the physical world.
cards.body:
Jeff Bezos has launched Prometheus, a startup developing what the founder calls an "artificial general engineer" for the physical world. The company raised $12 billion in funding and is valued at $41 billion, making it one of the best-capitalized startups in the physical AI space.

Prometheus aims to create AI-powered engineering tools that can automate heavy engineering work and drug design by developing artificial intelligence systems capable of designing physical products. The startup enters a competitive field where multiple companies are pursuing similar goals of creating AI systems that operate in the physical world rather than purely digital environments.

cards.headline: Meta AI division faces internal turmoil as engineers report difficult working conditions
cards.teaser: The artificial intelligence unit employing 6,500 people has been described in negative terms by engineers working within the division.
cards.body:
Meta's artificial intelligence unit, which was established months ago and employs 6,500 people, is experiencing significant internal problems. A report characterizes the working environment in harsh terms, with engineers describing their experience in the division negatively.

The unit appears to be approaching a point of internal conflict, according to the report. The AI division represents a major investment for Meta, but the working conditions reported by engineers suggest organizational challenges. The scale of the unit, with thousands of employees, means any widespread dissatisfaction could affect Meta's AI development efforts.

cards.headline: NASA administrator addresses criticism of all-male Artemis III crew selection
cards.teaser: The space agency faced questions about the crew composition for the lunar mission scheduled for 2027.
cards.body:
Original card text retained

The provided sources do not contain sufficient verified information to rewrite the card. The Guardian source describes the Artemis III crew composition (Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and Luca Parmitano) and their mission role, but does not address the criticism or NASA leadership's response that is the focus of the original card. The BBC source is unrelated to this story. The New York Times headline is referenced but no article text is provided.

To rewrite this card accurately, I would need source material that actually covers NASA's response to the criticism about crew diversity.

hero.headline: Ghana's Partey denied entry to Canada, will miss World Cup opener
hero.teaser: Arsenal midfielder Thomas Partey will miss Ghana's opening match at the 2026 World Cup after being denied entry to Canada.
hero.body:
Thomas Partey will not play in Ghana's opening match of the 2026 World Cup against Panama after Canadian authorities denied him entry to the country. The Villarreal midfielder's absence represents a significant blow to Ghana's tournament hopes as they prepare for their fixture in Toronto.

The Arsenal academy product was charged with five counts of rape and one count of sexual assault in July 2025 by the Metropolitan Police. He pleaded not guilty to those charges. In February 2026, he faced two additional counts of rape and again pleaded not guilty to all charges.

Canadian immigration authorities have not publicly detailed the reasons for their decision to deny Partey entry. A spokesperson for Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada stated they would not comment on individual visa cases but explained that "applications are considered on a case-by-case basis based on the information presented by the applicant." The spokesperson added that all applicants must comply with eligibility and admissibility requirements regardless of nationality.

Fifa has attributed the denial to the Canadian government's decision, stating that the organization was not responsible for the visa rejection. The world football governing body has been contacted for additional comment on the matter.

The situation reflects broader concerns about player and official access to the 2026 World Cup, which is being held across the United States, Canada and Mexico. Several nations already face travel restrictions. Four World Cup qualifiers, including Haiti, Iran, Côte d'Ivoire and Senegal, are subject to some form of travel ban in the United States.

Palestinian Football Association officials have also been denied Canadian visas ahead of the Fifa Congress scheduled for April 30 in Vancouver. Three officials, including PFA president Jibril Rajoub, had their visa applications rejected. The PFA had planned to use the Congress to address concerns about Israeli football clubs playing in occupied Palestinian territory.

The denial of entry to multiple groups of officials and players has raised questions about access to the tournament. However, Fifa President Gianni Infantino has repeatedly insisted there will be no adverse effects on travel for teams or supporters during the competition. "Everyone will be welcome in Canada, Mexico and the United States for the Fifa World Cup," Infantino stated after a meeting of the Confederation of African Football last year.

Partey's absence will force Ghana's coaching staff to adjust their tactical approach for the crucial opening match. The midfielder had been expected to play a central role in Ghana's midfield during the tournament. His unavailability leaves the team without one of their most experienced players at a critical stage of the competition.

cards.headline: Astros' Alvarez hits grand slam and two-run homer in first inning
cards.teaser: Houston Astros designated hitter Yordan Alvarez produced a historic offensive display in the first inning against the Kansas City Royals on Friday night, hittin.
cards.body:
Yordan Alvarez delivered a dominant performance in the first inning Friday night, hitting both a grand slam and a two-run homer against the Kansas City Royals. The back-to-back home runs gave the Houston Astros an early commanding lead.

The feat showcased Alvarez's power-hitting prowess and gave the Astros a significant advantage in the game.

cards.headline: Dempsey criticizes Marsch over anthem comments
cards.teaser: Former United States soccer star Clint Dempsey responded sharply to Jesse Marsch's suggestion that some American players needed encouragement to sing the national anthem.
cards.body:
Clint Dempsey, the U.S. men's national team's joint all-time leading scorer, fired back at Jesse Marsch after the Canada coach suggested American players needed to be begged to sing the Star-Spangled Banner. Marsch made the comments while speaking to reporters ahead of Canada's World Cup opener, drawing a comparison while praising his own team's patriotic display.

Dempsey, expressing that it was an honor to represent his country, told Marsch to focus on his own squad. Marsch served as an assistant for the USMNT from 2010 to 2011, including at the 2010 World Cup in South Africa, before becoming Canada's coach two years ago.

cards.headline: Boone says Yankees will not apologize to Chapman
cards.teaser: Yankees manager Aaron Boone stated the team does not owe Aroldis Chapman an apology for how they handled his departure at the end of the 2022 season.
cards.body:
Aaron Boone addressed comments made by Boston Red Sox pitcher Aroldis Chapman, who repeated his belief that the Yankees owe him an apology for his treatment at the end of the 2022 season. The Yankees manager said Friday that he does not believe an apology is necessary.

Chapman's departure from New York following the 2022 campaign has remained a point of contention. The former Yankees closer signed with Boston and has continued to express dissatisfaction with how the organization handled the end of his tenure in pinstripes.

cards.headline: Spurs coach Johnson expresses confidence in Fox after Game 4 struggles
cards.teaser: San Antonio coach Mitch Johnson voiced support for De'Aaron Fox following the guard's difficult performance in Game 4.
cards.body:
Spurs coach Mitch Johnson publicly backed De'Aaron Fox following the guard's poor performance in Game 4. Johnson addressed the media about Fox's struggles, emphasizing the team's continued faith in the player as the series moves forward.

The coach's show of support indicates the Spurs plan to maintain Fox in a prominent role heading into Game 5, despite his recent difficulties on the court.

cards.headline: Retired Lions center Ragnow explains decision to stop playing
cards.teaser: Former Detroit Lions center Frank Ragnow discussed the physical issues that led to his abrupt retirement announcement last year.
cards.body:
Frank Ragnow stepped away from the NFL one year ago with an abrupt retirement announcement on social media. The former Lions center has now opened up about that decision, revealing that his body simply told him it was time to stop playing football.

After initially retiring, Ragnow attempted an in-season return but failed a physical examination, which ultimately ended any hopes of coming back. The health setback made his retirement permanent.

cards.headline: Federal judge allows White House UFC event to proceed
cards.teaser: A judge ruled Friday that the White House can host a UFC event on Sunday in a ring constructed on the South Lawn.
cards.body:
A federal judge ruled Friday to allow the White House to proceed with a UFC event scheduled for Sunday. US District Judge Amit Mehta refused to block the mixed martial arts competition, which will take place in an elaborate ring already constructed on the South Lawn.

The event is being held to celebrate the nation's 250th anniversary and coincides with President Donald Trump's 80th birthday. The ruling clears the way for the unprecedented use of White House grounds for a professional combat sports competition.

hero.headline: Justice Department Approves Warner Bros Sale to Paramount in $111 Billion Deal
hero.body:
The Trump administration's Justice Department has approved Paramount Skydance's $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, clearing a major regulatory hurdle for the merger. The antitrust division completed its review after eight months of investigation, determining the deal would not harm competition or consumers.

The Justice Department stated it examined the merger's potential effects across three areas: streaming video on demand, linear television, and studio development and distribution of theatrical films. "The Division has completed its analysis of the proposed merger of Paramount and Warner Bros and determined based on the evidence received in its investigation that the transaction is not likely to result in harm to competition or American consumers," the agency said in its Friday announcement.

The Ellison family controls Paramount Skydance, which owns CBS News. Warner Bros Discovery operates CNN, HBO, and other major media properties. The combined company will control a significant portion of American media assets, including multiple film studios, television networks, streaming platforms, and news operations.

Paramount welcomed the approval, stating the merger would create a stronger company capable of competing against dominant technology platforms. "This deal is pro-competitive, resulting in a stronger company better positioned to compete against dominant technology platforms in an industry increasingly defined by intense competition for audiences, talent, technology, and investment," the company said.

However, significant hurdles remain. The UK's Competition and Markets Authority has opened its own investigation, setting an August 7 deadline to determine whether further review is needed. European regulators are also investigating the funding behind the deal, as three Gulf sovereign-wealth funds have committed a combined $24 billion.

Australia has already approved the merger, determining it would not substantially lessen competition in theatrical film distribution.

Several groups have opposed the deal. Journalists at both CBS News and CNN have expressed concerns about potential network consolidation, which could trigger significant job cuts. The companies have projected $6 billion in synergies from the merger. Some CNN staff have worried that Larry Ellison, a longtime Trump associate, and his son David could push the network in a different editorial direction, though David Ellison pledged in March that CNN's editorial independence would be protected.

California Attorney General Rob Bonta indicated his office continues investigating the merger. "The merger of Warner Bros and Paramount is not a done deal and remains under investigation by my office," he posted on social media.

Critics have also questioned the approval's legitimacy. Free Press co-chief Craig Aaron stated the decision showed bias, saying Paramount had "fêted, flattered and promised sweeping changes to news coverage to win the administration's approval." Democrat Senator Elizabeth Warren called the approval "terrible news for every American who doesn't want Trump-aligned billionaires to control what they watch."

A coalition of state attorneys general could potentially file a lawsuit to block the merger in coming weeks.

cards.headline: Film Critic Gene Shalit Dies at 100
cards.teaser: Gene Shalit, the longtime film critic known for his appearances on the Today show, has died at age 100.
cards.body:
Gene Shalit, the longtime movie critic for NBC's Today show, died at age 100. Known for his distinctive appearance—his puffy hair and oversized handlebar mustache—Shalit became a familiar fixture on television for over four decades.

Shalit joined Today in 1970 and became arts editor in 1973. He was celebrated for his wit and intelligence, earning recognition as a middle-of-the-road critic who delighted audiences with pun-filled reviews. His affection for wordplay and humor made him one of the most recognizable film critics in American media.

cards.headline: Directors Guild Secures Limits on Non-Directors Taking TV Jobs in New Contract
cards.teaser: The Directors Guild of America negotiated a provision restricting actors and others from directing television episodes as part of a new four-year contract.
cards.body:
The Directors Guild of America secured a provision in its new contract that limits actors and other crew members from directing episodes of television series. The measure aims to preserve jobs for career television directors amid a 40 percent decline in production jobs over the past four years.

The guild reached a tentative four-year agreement with major studios and streaming companies. The contract also includes gains for the guild's health plan and increases to streaming residuals. The guild's board has approved the deal, which addresses concerns about employment levels in the television directing sector.

cards.headline: Olivia Rodrigo Releases New Album
cards.teaser: Olivia Rodrigo released a new album that includes love songs alongside her signature style.
cards.body:
Olivia Rodrigo's third album has generated significant media attention, with critics and gossip outlets alike scrutinizing its lyrics for personal references. The release comes following her breakup with British actor Louis Partridge late last year. One track, "Purple," was reportedly changed from a "very sweet and saccharine" love song to reflect the end of their relationship.

The album showcases Rodrigo's evolving musical style, drawing comparisons to The Cure's influence. Despite widespread speculation about the album's autobiographical elements, critics have praised the quality of her songwriting and emotional depth across the record.

cards.headline: World Cup Opening Ceremony Features Performances by Future and Tyla in Los Angeles
cards.teaser: The World Cup opening ceremony in Los Angeles included performances by Future, Tyla, Lisa, Anitta, and Rema.
cards.body:
The USA's World Cup opening ceremony at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles showcased an array of musical performances. Future and Tyla were among the headliners, with the duo declaring "Game Time" during their set. Lisa, Anitta, and Rema also performed their collaborative track "Goals" for the star-studded event.

Katy Perry delivered a touching performance of "Wonder" alongside 10-year-old singer Tius, with Lukas singing the opening and closing lines of the song.

cards.headline: Nick Reiner Seeks Access to Trust Fund for Legal Defense in Parents' Killing Case
cards.teaser: Nick Reiner, accused of killing his parents, requested use of a trust fund they established to pay for his legal defense.
cards.body:
Nick Reiner asked to access a trust fund left by his parents to cover his legal defense costs in the case where he faces charges for their killings. The trustee launched an investigation into the trust rules before agreeing to the payment request.

Reiner claimed his siblings reversed their commitment to fund his legal defense. His former attorney, Alan Jackson, left the case under circumstances that Jackson has now addressed publicly. Rob Reiner's son faces charges in connection with his parents' deaths.

cards.headline: WABC-TV Anchor Bill Ritter Steps Down After Alzheimer's Diagnosis
cards.teaser: Bill Ritter left his position anchoring Eyewitness News at WABC-TV after being diagnosed with early stage Alzheimer's disease.
cards.body:
Bill Ritter announced his departure from WABC-TV's 6 p.m. Eyewitness News broadcast after receiving an early stage Alzheimer's diagnosis. The longtime anchor made the announcement during Friday's newscast, marking the end of his tenure in the evening anchor chair.

Ritter had anchored the station's flagship 6 p.m. newscast for more than two decades, beginning in 2001. Medical tests led to his diagnosis, prompting his decision to step down from the role.

hero.headline: Trump administration blocks foreign access to Anthropic's advanced AI models
hero.teaser: Commerce Secretary restricts international use of Anthropic's most powerful artificial intelligence systems in national security move.
hero.body:
The Trump administration is restricting foreign governments, companies and individuals from accessing Anthropic's most advanced AI models. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick announced the restrictions in a Friday letter to the company.

The move represents an escalation in how Washington treats cutting-edge AI as a national security asset. Anthropic now faces dual constraints: its technology is blacklisted for U.S. government use while also being restricted from foreign entities. The administration is prioritizing American advantage in AI development and preventing adversaries from accessing the most capable systems.

cards.headline: Trump announces US military killed Venezuelan gang leader in strike
cards.teaser: President Trump announced late Friday that U.S.
cards.body:
President Trump announced Friday that U.S. Southern Command conducted a strike that killed Niño Guerrero, leader of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua. Trump described it as a "swift and lethal kinetic strike" and shared a video appearing to show the airstrike on his Truth Social platform.

Tren de Aragua originated in Venezuela and has expanded operations across multiple countries. The gang has been linked to human trafficking, drug smuggling, and violent crime across South America and the United States, prompting increased concern from U.S. law enforcement and national security officials.

cards.headline: Appeals court denies Trump bid to keep name on Kennedy Center
cards.teaser: Federal panel allows deadline to proceed for removing president's name from arts venue exterior.
cards.body:
A federal appeals court in Washington rejected an emergency appeal from the Trump administration seeking to pause the removal of Trump's name from the Kennedy Center's facade. Justice Department lawyers filed the appeal on Friday, but the court denied the request, allowing the deadline for removal to proceed.

The ruling means Trump's name must be removed from the exterior of the performing arts venue as previously ordered by a lower court. The case centers on the authority to modify building exteriors and naming rights at federally supported cultural institutions.

cards.headline: Justice Department approves Paramount acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery
cards.teaser: DOJ clears $110 billion merger between entertainment giants after antitrust review.
cards.body:
The Department of Justice has approved Paramount's $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, clearing a major regulatory hurdle for the deal. The antitrust review determined the transaction would not harm competition or consumers.

The merger combines Paramount and CBS with Warner Bros. Discovery's holdings, including HBO and CNN. However, the deal still faces scrutiny in the UK and potential lawsuits from state attorneys general. Critics in the entertainment industry worry the consolidation will reduce competition among film studios and result in the merger of two major news networks—CBS News and CNN.

cards.headline: Democrat calls for testimony on White House handling of Epstein files
cards.teaser: House Oversight Committee member requests questioning of Vice President Vance and officials over reported containment effort.
cards.body:
Rep. Robert Garcia pressed House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer to call Trump administration officials for testimony following a report on the White House's efforts regarding Jeffrey Epstein files. The California Democrat sent Comer a letter urging immediate steps to bring in several officials for questioning. Garcia specifically requested testimony from Vice President Vance and other White House officials.

The request follows reporting about the administration's approach to the scandal surrounding convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Garcia's letter seeks congressional investigation into how the White House has handled information and documents related to Epstein. The House Oversight Committee has jurisdiction over executive branch operations and conduct.

cards.headline: Trump administration limits Census Bureau data releases
cards.teaser: Officials restrict methods for protecting privacy in public statistics, potentially reducing available data.
cards.body:
The Trump administration is restricting the Census Bureau's privacy protection methods when releasing statistical data. Officials say the changes aim to reduce "statistical noise" in Census publications. The shift could decrease the amount of public data available for redistricting and other purposes.

The Census Bureau employs various techniques to safeguard individual privacy while publishing aggregate demographic and economic information. Redistricting efforts, government agencies, and research organizations depend on detailed Census data to track population changes and guide resource allocation decisions.

cards.headline: Trump tells Netanyahu he expects to sign Iran deal within days
cards.teaser: President informs Israeli prime minister of impending agreement, signaling end to joint military campaign.
cards.body:
President Trump called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday evening to inform him he expected to sign a deal with Iran within days. Trump told Netanyahu the agreement was final and it was time to end the war, according to a senior U.S. official. The call delivered news Netanyahu did not want to hear about the direction of U.S. policy.

Netanyahu had hoped the war would lead to regime change in Tehran when he joined military operations alongside Trump. The prime minister faces an election four months away and had envisioned a different outcome from the campaign. The pending agreement represents a shift in U.S. approach toward Iran and ends the joint military effort that Netanyahu had supported.
